title: MR Vaccine

blocks.text:
The MR vaccine is an immunization that provides protection against two infectious diseases: measles and rubella (German measles).

The MR vaccine is actually part of the MMR vaccine (Measles, Mumps, and Rubella). In Indonesia, however, the mumps component is administered separately because mumps has become relatively uncommon in the country.

Meanwhile, both measles and rubella continue to occur frequently, particularly among children. Rubella also requires special attention during pregnancy, as infection in early pregnancy may lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, or congenital abnormalities in the baby.

For this reason, MR vaccination is recommended for children to protect them against both diseases and to help prevent transmission within the community.
Who Should Receive the MR Vaccine?

The MR vaccine is recommended for all children from 9 months up to under 15 years of age during the national MR immunization program.

The vaccine is administered by a healthcare professional through an injection into the upper arm or thigh.

Children who have previously received a measles vaccine should still receive the MR vaccine to provide additional protection against rubella.

In addition to children, the MR vaccine is also recommended for women who are planning a pregnancy.

According to the Indonesian Ministry of Health, the MR vaccine used in Indonesia has been recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) and approved by the Indonesian Food and Drug Authority (BPOM).

The vaccine has also been used safely in more than 141 countries worldwide.

Most people experience no significant side effects after receiving the MR vaccine.

When side effects do occur, they are generally mild and temporary, such as mild fever, skin rash, or pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site.

These reactions are normal and usually resolve within 2 to 3 days.

blocks.text:
In very rare cases, a child may experience an allergic reaction after receiving the MR vaccine.

Vaccination works by introducing weakened or inactivated components of disease-causing organisms, allowing the immune system to recognize them and develop protection against future infection.

Some individuals who are particularly sensitive to vaccine components may experience a severe allergic reaction known as anaphylaxis. Although extremely rare, this condition requires immediate medical attention and is generally treatable when managed promptly.

For this reason, parents are encouraged to consult a doctor before vaccination, especially if their child has a history of severe allergies.
Does the MR Vaccine Cause Autism or Paralysis?

No.

There is no scientific evidence that the MR vaccine, or any other routine childhood vaccine, causes autism or paralysis.

Claims linking vaccination to autism or paralysis have been thoroughly investigated and disproven by health experts and scientific studies worldwide.

In rare situations where autism or paralysis is diagnosed after vaccination, the timing is purely coincidental. Through appropriate medical evaluation and laboratory testing, healthcare providers are able to identify the actual underlying cause of the condition.

Vaccination is not considered a cause of autism or paralysis.
Who Should Not Receive the MR Vaccine?

Although the MR vaccine is safe for most individuals, not everyone is eligible to receive it. Individuals with certain medical conditions or specific contraindications should consult a healthcare professional before vaccination to determine whether the vaccine is appropriate for them.
